paragraphs.heading: Clocks inside rocks
paragraphs.text: Radiometric dating, also called radioactive or radioisotope dating, finds the age of materials such as rocks that took in traces of radioactive impurities when they formed. It compares how much of a natural radioactive isotope is in the material with how much of its decay products there is. Those products build up at a known, constant rate. Ernest Rutherford (1906) and Bertram Boltwood (1907) pioneered the method for minerals and rocks.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Today it is the chief way to learn how old rocks and other geological features are in absolute terms, including fossils and the Earth itself. Used together with stratigraphic principles, it helps set up the geologic time scale, which in turn tells us about the ages of fossils and the inferred pace of evolutionary change. It also dates archaeological materials such as ancient artifacts, and helps trace where meteorites and asteroids came from. Among the best-known versions are radiocarbon, potassium–argon and uranium–lead dating.

paragraphs.heading: Unstable atoms
paragraphs.text: Every chemical element has an atomic number, which is the number of protons in the nucleus of its atoms. An element can also come in different isotopes, which differ in their number of neutrons, and one particular isotope of one particular element is called a nuclide. Some nuclides are unstable: sooner or later an atom will decay on its own and turn into a different nuclide. This can happen through alpha decay, beta decay, or splitting into two or more nuclides.

paragraphs.heading: Half-lives and decay chains
paragraphs.text: No one can predict when one particular nucleus will decay, but a large collection of them shrinks exponentially at a rate described by its half-life. After one half-life, half of the atoms have become a "daughter" nuclide. Often the daughter is radioactive too, giving a decay chain that ends in a stable daughter, and the longest half-life in the chain is usually the one that counts. Systems used for dating have half-lives from about 10 years, as in tritium, to over 100 billion years, as in samarium-147.

paragraphs.heading: A steady clock
paragraphs.text: For most radioactive nuclides the half-life depends only on the nucleus and is essentially constant. Temperature, pressure, chemical surroundings and magnetic or electric fields do not change it. The only exceptions are nuclides that decay by electron capture, such as beryllium-7, whose rate can be affected by the local density of electrons. For all the others, the balance between the original nuclide and its decay products shifts predictably, so it can serve as a clock running from the moment the nuclides entered the material.

paragraphs.heading: Checking the answer
paragraphs.text: The basic equation only works if neither the parent nuclide nor its daughter entered or left the material after it formed. So it is vital to learn as much as possible about the material and to look for signs of alteration, and taking samples from several places in the rock body improves precision. Different methods may also be compared. Rocks called the Amitsoq gneisses, in western Greenland, came out at 3.60 ± 0.05 billion years by uranium–lead dating and 3.56 ± 0.10 billion years by lead–lead dating, results that agree with each other.
